fields.sections.0.ko: The archaeological site discovered by the author's AI agents turned out to have already been recorded by archaeologists in academic journals. Since the agents missed it during literature searches, it is more of a rediscovery rather than a pure discovery, though interestingly it had not yet been entered into the official registry of Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH). Despite these process limitations, the remainder of the event flow still presents a meaningful case.
fields.sections.1.ko: While traveling in Peru, the author learned historical background and encountered the story of Hiram Bingham discovering Machu Picchu in 1911. Interestingly, Bingham was originally searching for a different city, Vilcabamba, but reached the famous archaeological site by chance with guidance from a local farmer. The author derived the idea for his project from the thought of how Bingham might have proceeded had modern advanced technology been available.
fields.sections.2.ko: The author consulted with multiple AI agents including Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok, and all recommended LiDAR technology. While satellite photographs show archaeological sites above the jungle as merely forests, LiDAR can precisely map structures beneath the surface by firing laser pulses through gaps between trees. Peru lacked LiDAR coverage, but the Maya region had much richer public data, so the author shifted the research focus to the Maya region.
fields.sections.3.ko: The author instructed the agents to analyze approximately 1,200 square kilometers of LiDAR imagery in the Maya region. 48 agents reviewed the images one by one, searching for pyramids, platforms, and plazas while filtering out natural hills, sinkholes, and roads. No special machine learning classifier was used; the agents made visual judgments directly following precise guidelines. After analyzing overnight, the author found that the agents had discovered numerous settlements and regular-shaped structures that appeared to be constructions.
fields.sections.4.ko: The author asked the agent to verify whether the discovered sites were already known by checking literature and records. The agent reported that one major settlement was not in the registry. This hillside at the cliff edge had structures with right angles and sharp edges that were visually identifiable as non-natural formations. In the enlarged images, a flat plaza, elliptical pyramids over 8-12 meters high, an adjacent high platform, and a flat depression presumed to be a rainwater reservoir were visible.
fields.sections.5.ko: Following the agent's advice, the author submitted a report to Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History. The author translated it to Spanish following Claude's suggestion and verified the original LiDAR point cloud to confirm that structures actually existed on the ground surface rather than vegetation. On October 21, a reply was received from INAH stating that "no registered archaeological site could be found at that location."
fields.sections.6.ko: According to the author's and agents' estimates, this site was a small civic center of the Classic Maya period (approximately AD 250–900), corresponding to a local elite urban center. The plaza was likely a public space where ceremonies or markets were held, the pyramid was a temple, and the adjacent high platform is presumed to have been the residence of the local ruler. Various other platforms in the surrounding area appear to be residential structures. A reconstruction image presented with 3D visualization shows the estimated appearance around AD 700.
fields.sections.7.ko: The author presented precedent cases of LiDAR technology being applied in archaeology. In 2024, archaeologists discovered an entire Maya city in Mexico using a similar method, and in 2025, another research team mapped settlements across the entire Maya lowlands, and this site was precisely included in that process. Ultimately, the site had already been documented by professional archaeologists in academic journals, and the author's agents had happened to reach the same location by chance.
fields.sections.8.ko: Because the author was not an archaeology expert, he could approach this task without preconceptions that it would be difficult. He simply selected an old problem, attempted the most intuitive method, and applied computational resources, yet reached the same results as experts, which in turn validates the approach. The author emphasizes that this case is not fundamentally about archaeology but rather an example demonstrating the broad applicability potential of AI agents.
fields.sections.9.ko: Until now, most agentic AI cases have concentrated in fields like coding, mathematics, and physics, but in reality they are applicable to a far broader range of areas. The author believes a revolution is imminent across all scientific fields, with the remaining bottlenecks being only curiosity, imagination, and computational capacity. Ultimately, the author suggests that it would be possible to map the entire planet with LiDAR and have agents discover the remaining sites.
fields.caveat: The author is not an archaeology expert, the discovery ultimately turned out to be a rediscovery rather than a discovery, and the accuracy of LiDAR data interpretation is based on estimation, so this should be read with these factors in mind.
